evidence.from: research/dlab/candidates.jsonl as committed at a286851 (660 classed rules); nothing was run on any data for this

plan: What the 660 rules say together (the analysis is to be written to docs/RESEARCH_META_ANALYSIS.md by a script, from the committed record): on the perpetuals there is information before costs and none after; on the funds and on energy there is none before costs either.

One hypothesis follows from that and is not yet testable: costs are paid on net trades. The lab charges every part of a book its own costs, so a book of many rules on the same instruments pays for trades that would cancel. Charged on the net position of each instrument, the whole population of rules the scan kept on the fit rows (no choice on the check rows) may keep part of its gross expectancy. It needs new code in the lab (a book whose costs are netted, with tests on built markets), a new lab version, and then one submission for the perpetuals only, flagged as formed after seeing the check rows. My estimate of its chance to reach the bar in a 2.3-year validation window is 5 to 10 in a hundred: enough for a free place, not for one that raises the bar.
Nothing is proposed for the funds or for energy: there is no gross expectancy to protect from costs.
The two paper systems come first (the owner's newest order): a reconciled audit of TRND-1 and RADAR-1, and one controlled experiment on RADAR-1's churn, judged on its later trades.

about: The plan of 2026-11-14: a book of the whole population of the perpetuals' rules with its costs charged on net trades
decision: SET ASIDE: the new lab code it needs is not built, and no submission is made.

evidence.arithmetic: Netting can at best divide the costs by the square root of the rules on an instrument (about 52: a factor of 7) and in practice by 2 to 3. At a correlation of 0.05 and costs divided by 3 the book stands at t 1.3 on the check rows, and the same on 852 validation rows gives about 1.4 against a bar of 3.0. Only with no correlation at all between 262 rules on 55 coins that move together would it reach the bar, and it would reach it before costs as well: the cost is not what stands between this population and the bar. My estimate of 5 to 10 in a hundred was too high: 1 to 5 in a hundred.
evidence.figures: On the check rows, a day and per unit of capital: +3.83 bp before costs, 4.37 bp of costs when each rule pays its own, -0.53 bp after. A t-statistic needs the book's spread, which depends on how the rules' daily P&L move together. If they were independent the spread would be 17 bp and the book's t before any cost 6.0; at an average correlation of 0.05 it is 51 bp and the t before any cost is 2.0; at 0.10 it is 1.5.
evidence.from: research/dlab/candidates.jsonl as committed at d1b4967; nothing was run on any data for this
evidence.population: the 262 rules of DLAB-CRD-1 and DLAB-CRD-D1 that are not closed families, the capital shared by family and then by rule: no choice on the check rows

why: The lab asks for three chances in a hundred before it spends a place that costs the bar nothing, and for new, tested code before a new kind of book. This does not clearly reach the first and would cost the second. It is recorded so that it is not rediscovered as an idea: it can be reopened by a reason to expect the rules' P&L to be nearly independent, and by nothing else.
